alt: The Mueller-Lyer illusion: two equal horizontal segments, the top one with fins pointing inward and the bottom one with fins pointing outward. A ruler underneath with dashed guides from the segment ends shows both segments have the same length.
Table of circle regions for 1 to 10 points: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 57, 99, 163, 256. A doubling guess column, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, is crossed out from 6 points on.

Side view of a three-legged stool and a four-legged chair on a floor drawn with a front and a back edge. All three stool feet touch the floor, marked with dots. The chair stands where the floor dips slightly: three of its feet touch the floor and its front right foot hangs above the dip, with a small arrow across the gap.

A laser pointer drawn as a cylinder lying on its side: a rounded back end, a push button on top and a ringed lens end on the right. A straight beam leaves the lens and runs to the right, ending in an arrowhead. A dot at the lens is labeled endpoint.

Cross-section of part of Earth with its center at the bottom. Parallel sunlight lines come straight down. At Syene a vertical well is lit to the bottom. At Alexandria a stick stands straight up from the ground, pointing away from Earth's center, and casts a short shadow. At the top of the stick, the angle between the stick and the sunlight is 7.2 degrees, the same as the angle at Earth's center between the radii to the two cities.
An eye at the vertex of a thin angle formed by two rays. A small near circle labeled Moon and a large far circle labeled Sun both fit exactly inside the same angle. Marked NOT TO SCALE.

Three line drawings. A salt crystal drawn as a cube with one shaded face. A virus shell drawn as an icosahedron. A cube with its 8 corners dotted and hidden edges dashed, with the count 8 corners, 12 edges, 6 faces and 8 minus 12 plus 6 equals 2.
Pascal's triangle, rows 0 to 7, written in a honeycomb. Every odd entry sits in a black-outlined hexagon; even entries have no outline. The outlined cells form stage 3 of the Sierpinski triangle.

Top view of a post at the center of a circle. The morning shadow and the afternoon shadow both reach the circle. Equal compass arcs from the two shadow tips meet on the halfway line, and a dashed ray from the post through that point is labeled N for north.

Two compasses side by side above a page line. Left, Euclid's compass: lifted off the page, its legs snap shut, shown by curved arrows. Right, our compass: lifted, it holds its opening, shown by a dashed line between the tips. Labels: Euclid's compass and our compass.
A paper scroll with rolled ends reading: A point is that which has no part. An arrow points to the word part, with a question mark at its tail.

A checklist with three conditions, orbits the Sun, nearly round and cleared its path, and two columns, Earth and Pluto. Earth gets a check on all three. Pluto gets checks on the first two and a cross on cleared its path.
A globe with its equator. A triangle runs from the North Pole down two meridians a quarter turn apart to the equator and is closed along the equator. Right-angle marks sit at all three corners.

The Mueller-Lyer illusion: two equal horizontal segments, the top one with fins pointing inward and the bottom one with fins pointing outward. A ruler underneath with dashed guides from the segment ends shows both segments have the same length.
Table of circle regions for 1 to 10 points: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 57, 99, 163, 256. A doubling guess column, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, is crossed out from 6 points on.

A table with columns n, guess and new rule. Guess is n squared plus 2n plus 2; the new rule adds n(n minus 1)(n minus 2). For n = 0, 1, 2 both columns read 2, 5, 10. At n = 3 the guess gives 17 and the new rule gives 23, which is boxed.

The rule 'true for every x'. Ana's 100 cases that work are shown as a 10 by 10 grid of check marks, with no proved badge. Ben's one failing case is circled. Revealed: 100 checks are not a proof; not every x works, so the rule is false.

Side view of a three-legged stool and a four-legged chair on a floor drawn with a front and a back edge. All three stool feet touch the floor, marked with dots. The chair stands where the floor dips slightly: three of its feet touch the floor and its front right foot hangs above the dip, with a small arrow across the gap.

Cross-section of part of Earth with its center at the bottom. Parallel sunlight lines come straight down. At Syene a vertical well is lit to the bottom. At Alexandria a stick stands straight up from the ground, pointing away from Earth's center, and casts a short shadow. At the top of the stick, the angle between the stick and the sunlight is 7.2 degrees, the same as the angle at Earth's center between the radii to the two cities.

Cross-section of part of Earth with its center at the bottom. Parallel sunlight lines come straight down. At Syene a vertical well is lit to the bottom. At Alexandria a stick stands straight up from the ground, pointing away from Earth's center, and casts a short shadow. At the top of the stick, the angle between the stick and the sunlight is 7.2 degrees, the same as the angle at Earth's center between the radii to the two cities.

Three line drawings. A salt crystal drawn as a cube with one shaded face. A virus shell drawn as an icosahedron. A cube with its 8 corners dotted and hidden edges dashed, with the count 8 corners, 12 edges, 6 faces and 8 minus 12 plus 6 equals 2.

Three line drawings, each with a checklist of two items, straight sides and no crossings. Circle: fails straight sides, passes no crossings. Bow-tie: passes straight sides, fails no crossings. Triangle: passes both. The marks appear with the answer.

Top view of a post at the center of a circle. The morning shadow and the afternoon shadow both reach the circle. Equal compass arcs from the two shadow tips meet on the halfway line, and a dashed ray from the post through that point is labeled N for north.

A drafting compass with its needle on one end of a segment and its pencil on the other end. Below, the same compass with the same opening stands at a new point and sweeps an arc. Caption: UNCHANGED OPENING. No numbers.
A paper scroll with rolled ends reading: A point is that which has no part. An arrow points to the word part, with a question mark at its tail.

Two boxes, point and line. An arrow labeled uses goes from point to line, and another labeled uses goes from line back to point, making a loop. Below, a separate list: starting words point and line, with no definition, and rules, the postulates about point and line.

A dictionary chain of four word boxes: point, then location, then position, then place, with an arrow from each word to the word its definition uses. A final arrow runs from place back up to point. Revealed caption: the definitions loop back.

Two columns, System A and System B. System A starts with the words point, line and between and assumes rules R1, R2 and R3. System B starts with point, line and distance and assumes rules R1 and R4. Revealed: a Proved row lists R2 under System B, so R2 is assumed in A but proved in B.

Truth table with columns P, Q, if P then Q, and if not Q then not P. Rows TT, TF, FT, FF. Both if columns read T, F, T, T. Revealed: the F in each if column is boxed and a caption says the two columns match.

Table of the four rows (P, Q) = (T, T), (T, F), (F, T), (F, F), with columns if P, then Q and if Q, then P. The first column reads T, F, T, T and the second reads T, T, F, T. Each F is boxed separately: row (T, F) breaks if P, then Q; row (F, T) breaks if Q, then P.

Truth table with columns P, Q, if P then Q, and if not Q then not P, and rows TT, TF, FT, FF. The two if columns are blank at first. Revealed: both read T, F, T, T, so the statement and its contrapositive match.

A checklist with three conditions, orbits the Sun, nearly round and cleared its path, and two columns, Earth and Pluto. Earth gets a check on all three. Pluto gets checks on the first two and a cross on cleared its path.

Two number cards, (1, 1, 1) and (0, 2, 3), under the test one zero, two positive. Each card has three boxes, one under each number. Revealed: (1, 1, 1) gets greater than 0 in all three boxes and is not balanced; (0, 2, 3) gets equal to 0, greater than 0, greater than 0 and is balanced.

A proof chain. u and v odd; by definition, u = 2a + 1 and v = 2b + 1; by substitution, u + v = 2a + 2b + 2; by the distributive property, u + v = 2(a + b + 1); because integers add to integers, a + b + 1 is an integer; by definition, u + v is even.

Kim's four lines on separate cards, in her random order: m + n = 2(r + s); m = 2r; so m + n is even; n = 2s. Each card has a grip for dragging. Revealed: order numbers 3, 1, 4, 2, putting the definitions first, then the algebra, then the conclusion.

A blank two-column table headed Statements and Reasons, with five empty rows. Revealed: m = 4r, n = 4s by definition of multiple; m + n = 4r + 4s by substitution; m + n = 4(r + s) by the distributive property; r + s is an integer because integers add to integers; so m + n is a multiple of 4 by definition of multiple.

Two number cards, 2 and negative 2, and the factoring x squared minus y squared equals (x minus y)(x plus y). Revealed: 2 squared is 4 and negative 2 squared is 4; if x squared equals y squared the product is 0, so x minus y = 0 or x plus y = 0, which gives x = y or x = negative y.

Arrow diagram. Left: a chain of arrows runs from a box labeled given, through two steps shown as dots, to a box labeled conclusion. Right: a box labeled conclusion with a loop arrow from the box back to itself. Revealed: the loop is crossed out.

Equation chain under a boxed note: n must be an integer. 2n + 1 = 8; subtract 1: 2n = 7; divide by 2: n = 7/2. 7/2 is not an integer, which clashes with the boxed note, marked by a crossed link and the word contradiction. Final boxed conclusion: no integer n solves 2n + 1 = 8.

A proof outline of three boxes joined by arrows: assume the opposite, then clash, then reject the opposite. Revealed: the reject the opposite box is outlined heavily as the end of the proof, and the wrong idea, prove the opposite is true, is crossed out.

Text panel. The goal, some label is wrong, sits above Ivy's start, every label is wrong, with the quantifier words underlined and lined up. Revealed: Ivy's line is crossed out as not the opposite, and the opposite is written beneath: no label is wrong, meaning every label is correct.
A globe with its equator. A triangle runs from the North Pole down two meridians a quarter turn apart to the equator and is closed along the equator. Right-angle marks sit at all three corners.

Three separate dots P, Q and R with no lines drawn between them, and a table whose columns are the lines {P, Q}, {Q, R} and {P, R} and whose rows are the pairs PQ, QR and PR. Each pair gets exactly one check, under its own line. Captions: every two points lie on exactly one line, which holds here; but each line has only two points, so this is not full Euclidean geometry.
Three labeled bins: ASSUMED, DEFINED and PROVED. The DEFINED bin holds the card W means in both U and V. Revealed: the card everything in U is in V goes in ASSUMED, and the card U = W goes in PROVED.

A box labeled postulates at the top, standing alone with no arrow into T or L. Below, boxes T and L with an arrow labeled uses from T to L and another labeled uses from L back to T, a loop. Revealed caption: no arrow comes from the postulates, so neither T nor L is proved.

Three status boxes: CONJECTURE, POSTULATE and THEOREM. The arrow from CONJECTURE into THEOREM is labeled needs a proof from the current postulates. Revealed: an arrow from CONJECTURE to POSTULATE labeled openly add, the system changes.

Points A, B and C in a row. Below, three panels labeled segment AB, ray AB and line AB, blank at first. Revealed: the segment joins A to B with endpoint dots and C off it; the ray starts at A, passes B and C, and has one arrow; the line passes through A, B and C with arrows at both ends.

Segment AB labeled AB = 5, and a ray from P through X. Revealed construction: a compass arc centered at A through B sets the opening; an arc of the same radius centered at P crosses the ray at Q; PQ = 5. The construction arcs stay visible.

A table with four point rows A, B, C, D and two line columns {A, B} and {C, D}, blank at first. No arrowheads. Revealed: A and B are checked under {A, B}, C and D under {C, D}; each point is on exactly one line, and no line holds all four points.

Three inventory cards, C1, C2 and S, each with columns COMPASS and METAL. C1: compass yes, metal yes. C2: compass yes, metal yes. S: compass no, metal yes. Revealed: the S card is outlined heavily; S is metal but not a compass, so every metal object is a compass is false.

A blank table with columns P marked and P on l and four rows. Revealed: the rows read T T, T F, F T, F F, with columns S, T, U giving F in at least one place in every row, so all three cannot hold together. Dropping U leaves row 1, dropping T leaves row 4, dropping S leaves row 2.

An arrow chain A to B to C, with an empty table of truth values for A, B, C below it, and a second empty table for A implies B, B implies C and C implies A. Revealed: a curved arrow shows A implies C; the values A false, B false, C true make A implies B and B implies C true but C implies A false, which is boxed.

The rule if the switch is on, then the lamp is on, above four observation cards written in words: SWITCH OFF, LAMP OFF; SWITCH OFF, LAMP ON; SWITCH ON, LAMP ON; SWITCH ON, LAMP OFF. Revealed: the last card is outlined heavily and breaks the rule; the second card, lamp on with switch off, is allowed.

The database test x + y = 1 above a table with columns PAIR, SUM and PRODUCT, blank at first. Revealed rows: (2, negative 1) has sum 1 and product negative 2; (2, 1/2) has sum 2.5 and product 1. Below: false positive (2, negative 1), false negative (2, 1/2), and a boxed exact test, xy = 1.

A blank table with point rows P, Q, R, S and line columns l, m, n. Revealed: l holds P, Q, R; m holds P, Q, S; n holds R and S. The P and Q checks under l and under m are outlined separately, and a caption says PQ lies on both l and m.
